title: Section 73: the power and its two hard limits
paras: So — section seventy-three. It lets you apply to develop land without complying with a condition on an earlier permission, and the authority then looks at one thing only — the conditions: it can grant with different ones, with none, or refuse if it thinks the originals should stand. It isn't a chance to reopen the principle of development. But it's judged against the development plan and material considerations as they stand at the date of the section seventy-three decision, which may have shifted since the original grant. One note before we start: the citations, case references and subsections all live in the written guide, so I'll stay on the ideas.

Two hard limits sit inside it. First, it's confined to conditions — you need an existing one to vary or remove. Second, and people forget this constantly, it cannot extend a permission's life: you can't push out the time for starting development, or for applying for reserved matters. Renewing a permission by varying its commencement condition is dead.

And a section seventy-three grant doesn't amend the original — it creates a new, free-standing permission alongside it. The original stays alive until it lapses, and the developer picks which to implement. Where the original's part-built, the new permission is for the whole development as varied, so it must be capable of coherent implementation across the whole site. Where two permissions cover the same land, Pilkington — coming up — decides whether implementing one bars the other. On timing: you can apply while the original's alive; after expiry it's unsettled, so prudently treat it as working on a subsisting permission — apply before it lapses, and don't assume an expired one can be revived.

title: The description limit: Finney and Armstrong
paras: Next, the single biggest constraint — Finney. Section seventy-three cannot alter the description of the development in the operative part. In Finney the permission described two wind turbines up to a hundred metres to the tip; a section seventy-three application tried to lift that to a hundred and twenty-five by varying a condition, and the Court of Appeal held the grant unlawful — the power reaches the conditions, not the description of what was permitted. So if the description has to change, section seventy-three is the wrong tool — you need a fresh application, or section seventy-three B once in force.

It gets called the route for a minor material amendment, but that's practice, not a legal limit. Armstrong confirmed there's no statutory ceiling on the extent of change. There the owner held permission for a single dwelling and applied to vary the approved-plans condition to redesign it; the authority and then an inspector refused as too material — and the High Court said they'd misdirected themselves. Materiality is irrelevant to whether the power's available, as long as the description — a single dwelling — stays unchanged and the varied conditions stay consistent with it.

Read together, one axis of the boundary is fixed: it isn't the size of the change that matters, it's consistency with the operative description. Even fundamental changes can go through section seventy-three, so long as you don't contradict the words describing the development. Which is why the original description sets the ceiling on a scheme's flexibility: a tight one — erection of fourteen dwellings in accordance with the approved plans — is a straitjacket, while a loose one — residential development — leaves room to vary substantially without a fresh application.

title: Fiske and Lambeth: conditions cannot negate or omit the grant
paras: Now the workaround that doesn't work — Fiske. If Finney stops you changing the description head-on, Fiske closes the dodge: you can't achieve by condition what you can't achieve to the description. The permission was for a solar farm with a substation — the operative part named it, the approved plans showed it, a condition required its details. A section seventy-three permission kept the word substation in the description but pulled it from the plans and deleted that condition, and the challenge succeeded. A permission is its operative part plus its conditions, and it's unlawful for a condition to derogate from or negate the grant — a permission that's internally inconsistent with its own operative part is bad.
Fiske also nailed a corollary decisive for phased schemes: a condition on one permission can't lawfully modify a separate permission. The grants are legally distinct. That comes back at drop-ins.

Reading a section seventy-three permission when a condition's left out got settled in Lambeth. The council varied one condition but, through a drafting error, failed to re-impose the one restricting a retail unit to non-food goods — and the Supreme Court held the use hadn't become unrestricted. Read as a whole, through a reasonable reader who knows the history, the limited description of the use fell to be read as if it were itself a condition, and the restriction survived. State that carefully: Lambeth is not authority that an omitted condition falls away — the Court reversed the Court of Appeal on exactly that. It's that the permission is construed in context, so a restriction can keep binding even unrestated. So the safe course is unchanged — re-state every condition you mean to continue, rely on neither its presence nor its absence, and issue a consolidated notice with the full description and the whole set of conditions as varied, so it reads as one document.

title: Section 73A: permission for what is already built
paras: Section seventy-three A next — permission for what's already built. A separate power, confused with section seventy-three over the numbering, but different: it authorises permission for development already carried out. Three situations — development with no permission at all; development that breached a condition; and development under a time-limited permission you want to keep beyond that period. And it can take effect from a date earlier than the grant, including when the work was done — that's what makes it genuinely retrospective, and it's the statutory basis of the retrospective planning application.

It comes up two ways — the landowner volunteering to regularise something built off-plan or an unauthorised change of use, or reacting to the threat or service of enforcement. And it overlaps with the ground A deemed application on an enforcement appeal, which invites the Secretary of State to grant permission for the development as carried out. So the choice between a proactive application and a ground A appeal comes down to cost, timing and appetite for risk.

Two cautions. Making the application isn't, in law, an admission that permission was required — but it's often treated as accepting the development's unauthorised, so don't do it reflexively. And it won't cure a permission never lawfully implemented: it grants a new permission, merits assessed afresh, and the authority can refuse, leaving the development open to enforcement. That's what clients struggle with — retrospective doesn't mean forgiven. It's weighed as if newly proposed, already standing there earns it no credit, and the money already spent forms no part of the balance.

title: Phased schemes: the whole-scheme problem
paras: Now, phased schemes — the whole-scheme problem. Big developments are rarely built exactly as first permitted: markets move, a phase gets re-planned, a house type's swapped, an access shifts. The instinct is section seventy-three — vary a condition and press on. For a single-permission masterplan that's now dangerous, because two independent lines of authority hem it in. One is the Finney and Fiske limit on section seventy-three itself. The other, more fundamental, is the Pilkington and Hillside rule that a permission for a multi-unit development is normally a single, indivisible whole — so a change to one part is, in law, a change to the entire permission.

Pilkington is the foundation. Where two permissions sit over the same land and it becomes physically impossible to carry out one because of what's been built under the other, the first can't lawfully be implemented or continued. The test is physical possibility on the ground, against what the earlier permission, read as a whole, authorised. It's why you can't hold overlapping permissions and build a hybrid of the lot — implement one and you may extinguish the ability to build the others. Sage adds the holistic reading: a permission authorises the development as a whole, not a string of independently lawful fragments, so you can't pick and choose parts and treat the built ones as separately authorised. A masterplan is a single integrated grant, not standalone consents plot by plot.

Put the two together and the trap is plain. The permission is one whole — Sage — and implementing an inconsistent later permission can make the original physically impossible to complete — Pilkington. So grabbing a separate consent for the troublesome phase and carrying on is precisely what can sterilise the original. Which brings us to the authority that pulled these threads together.

title: Hillside, Dennis and drop-in permissions
paras: So — Hillside, the decisive modern authority on amending large schemes. A permission from the sixties authorised four hundred and one dwellings on a twenty-eight-acre site to a detailed master plan; over the decades further permissions authorised departures until the original layout could no longer be built as approved, and the Supreme Court held it could no longer be relied on. Four propositions of general application. A multi-unit permission is normally one integrated whole, not a bundle of severable permissions. Where later development makes it physically impossible to complete the original as approved, the original can't lawfully be continued — Pilkington affirmed. The departure has to be material; a truly minor variation won't sterilise it. And severability is possible, but must be express on the terms of the particular permission — never presumed; the older authority allowing an expressly severable permission, F Lucas and Sons against Dorking, was left undisturbed.

Hillside also dealt with drop-in permissions — a separate consent for part of a site, standing in for a portion of the original. No blanket ban, but a drop-in doesn't amend the original, and implementing it may, through Pilkington, defeat your ability to complete the rest. The orthodox route to amend a large scheme is instead a section seventy-three application varying the whole permission — re-granting the entire development as amended — subject always to the Finney bar on the description.

Then Dennis tested the fallout. An estate regeneration consented by a phased outline permission; facing the Hillside problem, the developer used a section ninety-six A non-material amendment to insert the word severable, so a later drop-in wouldn't imperil the rest. The High Court held it wouldn't work: phasing on its own doesn't connote severability, and inserting the bare word severable doesn't make a permission severable. If it did, the implementation time limits would run separately for each phase — some could go time-expired, which nobody intended — and converting the permission to a severable one was a material change, well beyond section ninety-six A.

The lesson is stark: severability has to be engineered in from the outset by deliberate drafting — you can't retrofit it onto an existing phased consent. Drop-ins remain possible but hazardous, in three ways. One doesn't vary the original, which still needs completing as a whole. Once it's implemented, Pilkington and Hillside may leave the balance of the original incapable of lawful completion. And Fiske confirms a condition on the original can't authorise or accommodate the drop-in. So where you do pursue one, it should cover enough of the site to leave a coherent, implementable whole — and the assessment should address the combined development, not the parcel alone.

title: Choosing the route — and the coming s73B
paras: Finally, choosing the route — and the section seventy-three B that's coming. It follows from one question, asked first: does the change touch the description of development? If it does, section seventy-three is off the table — Finney — and it's a fresh application, or section seventy-three B once in force. If it doesn't, section seventy-three handles changes of any magnitude — Armstrong — provided the result is internally consistent, which is Fiske. Genuinely non-material changes go to section ninety-six A, but not one that inserts severability or is otherwise material — Dennis. Extending time for commencement or reserved matters is barred under section seventy-three, so that needs a fresh application. And regularising something already built is section seventy-three A, merits afresh, overlapping with a ground A appeal.

For a phased or masterplan scheme specifically, there are four realistic options right now. Vary the whole permission by section seventy-three — the orthodox Hillside route — which works only where the description's unchanged, per Finney, and consistent, per Fiske. A fresh full permission for the whole site, where the description must change or the scheme's moved substantially, sidestepping the Pilkington and Hillside trap by re-permitting the whole thing coherently. Engineer severability from the outset for new masterplans — after Dennis, the only reliable way to preserve flexibility. Or a carefully structured drop-in, viable in limited cases, with the safeguards we've covered and a clear-eyed read of the Pilkington risk to the remainder.

Section seventy-three B is inserted into the 1990 Act by the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act, and it's widely read as the intended answer to Hillside and Finney. It'll let you apply to vary an existing permission, including its description, provided the authority's satisfied the development as varied is not substantially different from what's already permitted — sitting between section ninety-six A and a fresh full application, giving large phased schemes a lawful route to material-but-modest amendment that section seventy-three can't deliver because of Finney. But it isn't in force yet — it's waiting on commencement regulations and the supporting procedure, fees and consultation. Until then those four options are the toolkit, and the Hillside analysis applies to every material change. The uncertain frontier, honestly, is the precise test for when a phased permission is severable: Hillside and Dennis establish it's possible and must be express — but not the drafting that reliably gets you there.
